intent: What should a Grand Strand homeowner check before replacing a whole lawn with artificial turf?
distinctValue: A lawn is the surface on a house lot most likely to push a lot past its hard-surface limit, and the one most likely to be dug near a large tree. The page gives the actual limits, how each city counts turf, and the tree rules that reach single-family lots. (1) North Myrtle Beach: the single-family district limits (R-1 40 percent, R-1A 45, R-1B, R-2 and R-3 50, R-2A and R-2B 60), and the R-1H Historic Low-Density Residential Overlay of Sec. 23-31(8), which allows 50 percent on parts of R-1. No other page on the site gives these limits or the overlay. The sizing step (add up hard surfaces, count the lawn as hard surface, then ask the city) is new; the staff remark from the 6 October 2025 minutes is quoted verbatim and limited to the 40 percent figure it names, with the reader told to get the city's answer for other districts. The full Sec. 23-129.4 test is left to the North Myrtle Beach town page; only the 'regardless of material type or labeling' clause, the owner's upkeep duty and the pool-basin exclusion are used, because the sizing step needs them. (2) Myrtle Beach: the Section 1603.B minimum pervious surface by district (50 percent in R-5, R-7, R-8, R-10 and R-15; 25 percent for a single-family house in RMM, RMH and RMV; no figure in the IR row, with the table note that other sections may still set one), the Sec. 203 pervious-surface definition, and the Section 903 tree rules as they apply to a lot with one single-family house: significant and landmark trees, the clearing/grubbing permit before vegetation alteration other than mowing, the extent of the tree protection zone (Sec. 203), what is prohibited in it, the loamy-soil requirement, the neighboring-tree coverage, the limited removal-permit reasons, and the tree survey and site-plan tree statement. No other page covers the Myrtle Beach pervious minimum or tree rules. (3) Horry County: the zoning code's Live Oak Protections, which Sec. 501.C and 503.C.3 apply to single-family lots, the 24-inch specimen live oak threshold and removal limits in Sec. 505.C, and the tree survey requirement in Sec. 505.A.1. No other page covers them. The page does not say whether county zoning reaches a lot inside a city; it tells the reader to ask. (4) North Carolina: one FAQ giving G.S. 143-214.7D(b)(6) and pointing to the state-line guide, which covers it in depth. Removed in the September 2026 repair because other pages already carry them: the Brunswick County block (NC vs SC guide), the soil-test FAQ (pet-turf page), the HOA recording FAQ with S.C. Code 27-30-130 (Longs page and HOA article), the rebate FAQ with the GSWSA watering tips (rebate guide), and the generic unincorporated-county drainage answer (pet-turf page). The earlier removal of claims resting on Internet Archive copies of horrycountysc.gov pages stands; the Horry County facts now on the page come from the county code on Municode, which loaded normally.

sources.label: City of Myrtle Beach Zoning Code (Appendix A), Article 2, Section 203, Definitions (current through 16 February 2026)
supports: Pervious Surface: Any material that permits full or partial absorption of stormwater or surface water directly into the ground.

Impervious Surface Coverage: The percentage of net land area of the lot covered by impervious surface. For the purpose of computing impervious lot coverage, the following items and like installations are considered impervious: building coverage, parking lots, parking structures, driveways, side-walks, patios, pool decks, wooden decks, grouted cut stone or tile walkways, and stone, shell or gravel surfacing.
Clearing: The removal of all vegetation.
Diameter-At-Breast-Height (DBH), Tree: The tree trunk diameter measured in inches at a height 4.5 feet above the ground ...
Tree Protection Zone: Generally 18 to 24 inches deep and extending a distance from the trunk to the dripline or equal to one-half the height of the tree, whichever is greater.

A text search of the Article 2 definitions page found no 'turf'. 'Synthetic' appears only in the head shop and synthetic marijuana definitions, and 'artificial' only in the grade, illumination, light source, light spillage, sign and irrigation definitions; no definition refers to artificial grass.

The code does not say whether removing a lawn is 'clearing' or 'vegetation alteration', so the page tells the reader to ask Construction Services.

sources.label: City of Myrtle Beach Zoning Code (Appendix A), Article 9, Section 903, Tree Protection (current through 16 February 2026)
supports: 903.A. Applicability. ... On lots containing only one single-family residence and its accessory uses in any Single-family (R) or Multifamily (RM) district, or residential Planned Unit Development (PUD) these regulations apply to only those trees defined as significant trees or landmark trees.

903.C. Significant Trees. The City hereby declares that the following are significant trees: Live Oak (Quercus virginiana), White Oak (Quercus alba), (Eastern Red Cedar (Juniperus virginiana), Southern Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora), and Bald Cypress (Taxodium distichum) trees with a 4" DBH or more.
903.D. Protected Trees. The City hereby declares that the following are protected trees: 1. Significant trees, as defined in section 903.C - Significant Trees;
903.E. Landmark Trees. ... Quercus virginiana Live Oak 25" ... Quercus alba White Oak 25"
903.G. Tree Removal Permits. It shall be unlawful to remove or otherwise destroy a protected tree or landmark tree without first obtaining a protected tree or landmark tree removal permit.

903.G.2. Criteria for issuance of protected or significant tree removal permits. Permits for the removal of a protected or significant tree may be issued for only the following reasons: a. Trees that are hazardous or cause safety-related problems; b. Diseased or infectious trees or trees in decline ... c. Trees or their root systems causing visible damage to structures, and/or areas used for pedestrian and vehicular traffic; ... g. Trees to be removed, pruned, or disturbed within the footprint or within ten feet of the footprint of buildings in Single-family residential (R) districts. h. Trees to be removed, pruned, or disturbed on plans approved by the Community Appearance Board or the Planning Commission whichever has final review responsibility and after all other applicable permits for construction have been issued.

903.H. Tree Survey. All applications for clearing, grubbing, grading, building, or demolition permits, or for any development or redevelopment of property shall include a tree survey sealed by a registered surveyor. ... 1. For all lots containing only one single-family residence ... the survey shall identify significant and landmark trees as requested by the Construction Services Department. a. If there is a tree located within the area to be constructed upon then location, type and DBH of the tree must be stated on the site plan.

903.L. Tree Protection During Clearing, Grubbing, and Development. Prior to the commencement of any site clearing or vegetation alteration, other than mowing, a clearing/grubbing permit shall be obtained from the Construction Services Department. All applications for clearing, grubbing, grading, building, or demolition shall include a Tree Protection Zone Plan (TPZ). The TPZ shall be designed to protect the trees and their roots on site as well as those on neighboring properties. Grading, filling, ditching and storage in the tree protection zone are prohibited. For all lots containing only one single-family residence and its accessory uses in Single-family (R), Multifamily (RM), or residential Planned Unit Development (PUD), a TPZ shall be designed to protect any and all significant and landmark trees.

903.L.3. Assurances that soil disturbance under the canopy of each tree will be limited to ANSI A300 (current edition) standards. Any soil added under the canopy of the tree must be a loamy soil mix to ensure compaction is minimized.

sources.label: N.C. Gen. Stat. 143-214.7D, Limitations on built-upon area requirements
supports: (b) For the purposes of implementing State or local government stormwater programs, none of the following surfaces shall be considered "built-upon area" or an impervious or partially impervious surface:
(6) Artificial turf, manufactured to allow water to drain through the backing of the turf, and installed according to the manufacturer's specifications over a pervious surface.
(c) The owner or developer of a property may opt out of any of the exemptions from "built-upon area" set out in subsection (b) of this section.

(d) Except as specifically required by federal law, a local government may not enact, implement, or enforce a local government ordinance, comprehensive plan, or stormwater program that establishes a definition of "built-upon area" or impervious surface that does not comply with subsection (b) of this section.
